Mr. Speaker, it is a difficult matter to speak in this chamber, even under ordinary circumstances; but I find it somewhat more difficult this afternoon following, as I do, the long and interesting statement which has been made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston).
In the short time at my disposal I shall not undertake to analyse the observations of the minister. He has given the house much information, and I am sure a great deal of it will be of interest not only to hon. members, but to the country in general. Listening to
the minister this afternoon, we must realize that in order to get the whole picture of Canada's activities in the war we must have reports, not only from one minister, but from all of them.
As was stated by the minister, the activities of the Department of National Defence depend upon the amount of work done by the Department of Munitions and Supply. He has pointed out that the work of one department, and his in particular, cannot move any faster than the progress of the Department of Munitions and Supply will permit.
It would appear that I am the first member who would be affected by the ruling which was made by Mr. Speaker this afternoon, at the opening of the sitting, to the effect that speeches are not to be read. I wish the ruling had been made at the beginning of the session and, indeed, I suggest it should have been made at that time. Personally, I am in full accord with it, and in the short time at my disposal I shall endeavour as nearly as possible to abide by it.
_ It is customary for hon. members speaking in the debate on the address in reply to compliment the mover and the seconder. Unfortunately I was not in the house when those hon. members delivered their speeches. I have, however, read them; I have listened to the observations of hon. members who followed them in the debate, and I have read newspaper comments, all of which satisfy me that the congratulations which have been heaped upon those hon. members have been merited.
I agree fully with the observations of my hon. leader who stated, in effect, that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) rather went out of his way to characterize those who advocate more and more assistance to Great Britain as being more English than the English. We of this party have always contended that the fullest possible support should be given to England, not only for the protection of Britain but because our own salvation depends upon England to-day as it has depended upon England in the past.
Before the war some hon. members rather scoffed at this idea; it has been interesting to see the change of heart on their part. I have heard some hon. members advocate strict neutrality; others, nationalism, and others have said that our defence depended upon the United States. We have heard all sorts of half-baked ideas advocated in this house during the last four or five years, but it would be a brave or bold member who would rise in his place to-day and give expression to the same ideas.
The Address-Mr. Brooks

I listened with much pleasure to the latter part of the address of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) delivered yesterday. After hearing that part of his speech I am ready to forgive him to some extent for many of the shortcomings of some of his previous speeches. I am sure there is none of us who does not share the feelings expressed by him. I was interested to hear his account of what has been going on in England during the last few months. We are all proud to know that while England is taking this terrific beating, her head is still high. The thought occurs to me, and I am sure it must have occurred to a great many other people, that if it had not been for a few thousand light-hearted and brave British boys in the British air force during the last few months, there might be a different story written for civilization and this empire of ours.
Yesterday I read in the press an article which brings to my mind another matter of which I shall speak in a moment. We all heard the eulogies of Mr. Chamberlain, and we all know how deserving they were. The article in yesterday's paper stated that the ashes of the late Prime Minister of Great Britain had been placed on the south side of Westminster Abbey beside the plain grey stone marking the burial place of Andrew Bonar Law, the Canadian-born Prime Minister of two decades ago. I would point out that from 1914 to 1918, when this empire was passing through one of the most serious times in its history, as it is to-day, it was a Canadian, born in New Brunswick, who stood next to Mr. Lloyd George in his efforts to protect and save the empire. I would point out also that to-day the man of whom we hear the most next to Mr. Churchill, the man who is doing the most to preserve this empire of ours, is another Canadian bom in New Brunswick. We all recognize the wonderful work that Lord Beaverbrook is doing for this empire of ours, and I am sure that we of the little province by the sea will be excused for the great pride we feel in this connection.
We are all greatly interested, not only in the raising of troops but in the providing of munitions and supplies. We feel that New Brunswick has not been receiving the same attention in this regard as have other parts of Canada. Week after week we receive reports from the director of public information giving the amount of money being spent in Canada on munitions and supplies. It is seldom that any mention is made of munitions or supplies being provided by New Brunswick. I submit that this is something which should be corrected. That province is particularly well situated for the manufacture of munitions to

be sent overseas. We are on, the Atlantic seaboard, and instead of munitions and supplies being manufactured in central and western Canada, they could very well be made in New Brunswick, and thus save the expense of a long rail haul.
It is true, as will probably be pointed out, that considerable work has been done upon the airfields of the maritime provinces. But this is for the protection of all of Canada. The government could hardly help avoid spending money upon these airfields. The minister mentioned that considerable money had been spent in my home town of Sussex; I think $1,800,000 was the amount he mentioned as having been expended upon the construction of huts. There have also been considerable expenditures at Debert, Nova Scotia. This is work which has to be done for general protection, and my request now is that more munitions should be manufactured in New Brunswick, thus giving more employment to our people.
I was glad to hear the Minister of Agriculture state that he had arranged a trade agreement with the United Kingdom whereby the farmers of Canada would1 be able to sell more of their farm products. But this agreement will be of little benefit to the farmers of the province from which I come. Our farmers are principally potato producers and dairymen. The United States trade agreement had an adverse effect upon the potato producers of New Brunswick, and to-day it is almost impossible for a man engaged in this type of agriculture to make a decent living for himself and his family. It is interesting to note that in western Canada the price set on wheat is a minimum one, but the price of dairy products has been pegged; the price set is a maximum one. There is a vast difference between setting a maximum price for one product and setting a minimum price for another.
Then, in connection with bacon, while the farmers of the maritime provinces are not large producers of this product, there is only one reason why they are not. They cannot get feed from western Canada at a reasonable cost because of the high freight rates. Everything seems to work against the prosperity of the people of my province and the other provinces by the sea. It is not because we are not deserving. Is it necessary for me to point out to this house that from 1914 to 1918 there was no more patriotic section in this whole Dominion of Canada than New Brunswick and the maritime provinces generally? The same is true to-day. If you look at enlistments in the overseas forces, you will find that the men of New

The Address-Mr. Brooks
Brunswick are enlisting in numbers comparable with those of any other part of this dominion, and I repeat that we are not receiving the attention which we deserve and to which we are entitled. It has been intimated that perhaps we do not press sufficiently for these things, so now I address myself to the members from New Brunswick who sit on the government side of the house. I have sat here for five years and I am of opinion that the Liberal members sitting in this House of Commons have not pressed the government hard enough on New Brunswick's behalf. I want to assure them that if they will make a concerted effort to impress our claims upon the government in season and out of season, both inside the house and outside they will have the whole-hearted support of every Conservative member from that province.
It has been rumoured, Mr. Speaker, that my good friend the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Michaud) is about to retire from parliament in order to accept an appointment to the bench of our province. It is not merely rumoured but I have seen it stated in the press. I congratulate the minister if such is the fact and I might add that in congratulating him I am doing a great deal more than I think some of his Liberal friends are doing in New Brunswick. If the minister leaves this chamber and the cabinet, it will be necessary for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), to appoint someone in his stead. I recall that the Prime Minister during the last election, and in speeches in this house since the election, said that he would select the best men he could get in this country for his cabinet. That should be the case. In times like these, the best men in the country are none too good. There are those who sit behind the Prime Minister who have ques- . tioned certain recent appointments which he has made, and I would ask the Prime Minister, when he selects a minister from New Brunswick, to select the best man he can possibly get from that province. Of course I know he has precluded himself from selecting anyone who is not of his own party. But we want strong representation in the cabinet from our province. This country needs strong representation, and if the best man is not in the house I ask the Prime Minister to go to the province and select there the very best man that can be obtained.
I wish to say a few words with reference to the training centres. First, let me say that I have had Charge of a training centre for the past thirty days. At the beginning of the war, having been in the militia and on the reserve for some years, I volunteered my
services either for overseas duty or at home, and just before the close of last session the district officer commanding the district from which I come telegraphed and telephoned me requesting that I take charge of a training centre in New Brunswick. I was glad to do so, and I suppose that as far as practical knowledge is concerned, I have as much knowledge of training centres as any man in this House of Commons.
A training centre was established at Fredericton. I had expected that there would be one training centre for the Whole province but two were established. I have no great criticism to make of two training centres being established, one at Fredericton and one at Edmundston. If I had any criticism to make it would be that at a time when we are talking of unity in this country and trying to bring our people together, a splendid opportunity was lost in New Brunswick, where we have many English-speaking and many Frenchspeaking young men, in not establishing only one training centre for the province where French and English-speaking boys could have come together and learned more about each others' opinions. This, however, was not done, and an English centre was established at Fredericton and the French one at Edmundston.
I was impressed by what the minister said as to the duty of our citizens to help entertain our soldiers in all parts of this dominion. I should like to pay tribute to the good people of Fredericton for doing everything they possibly could to help entertain the soldiers. The citizens gave us their bands for church parades; they opened their homes to the soldiers and provided them with entertainment.
I am speaking of training centres to-day from the point of view of the men who trained in them. There has been criticism levelled that the men who attended these training centres were an undisciplined mob. That term might have been applied to the men when they landed in camp the first day, coming from all over the province with their suitcases and civilian clothes, and some of them perhaps not knowing exactly why they were coming, but they could not possibly have been characterized as an undisciplined mob when they left camp thirty days later because they marched out with their chins up, just as fine a body of men as one could find anywhere.
There has been talk about these men being pampered. I think the government propaganda had something to do with that report giving the wrong impression across this country. I say emphatically that these men were not pampered nor did they wish to be pampered. If getting up at six o'clock in the morning, making your own bed, shaving and
The Address-Mr. Brooks

getting ready for breakfast at seven, and then after breakfast going out at eight o'clock and taking physical training and spending the whole day at drill-if that is being pampered, then these men were pampered. In addition, they had their fatigues to do. They made up their beds, rolled their blankets, cleaned out their huts, helped to wash the dishes and to scrub the floors; in fact, did all the work that men in barracks should do. I doubt whether any Canadian active service force unit in Canada during the first thirty days of their training, and perhaps much longer, made more progress or worked harder than did the men who were in these particular training centres.
I noticed in the Montreal Star a report that some men had come back from the training centres in certain parts of the province of Quebec and complained about the food. The ration in the training centres is the same as that given to the soldiers in every other camp in Canada. It is good, wholesome food, and I heard very little complaint. The fact is that unless a soldier is complaining he does not consider himself a soldier. Most of our wives will tell us that if we do not complain about the food at home they think there is something wrong with us, and if a body of men do not do a little complaining we would probably think there was something wrong with them.
But to give some idea of what benefit training is to the men and how they improve under the strict routine of military life, I had my medical officer, Captain Petrie, weigh and record the weights of men at different periods. The total weight gained from October 10 to November 6, roughly one training period, by 114 recruits examined for weight, was 648-5 pounds. Only one recruit, who had been sick for many days during the training period, lost one pound. The average gain per recruit for the training period was 5-68 pounds; which shows, as I say, that the military life and training are beneficial to the men.
I also have a summary from the medical officer regarding sick parades. The daily percentage of trainees on sick parade was 2-95 per cent. Por the training staff it was [DOT]63 per cent, or a total, for all, of 2-44 per cent. The total number of training days for the period for the unit was 25,800. The total hospital days for the unit numbered 239, and the percentage of training time lost on account of hospitalization was -93 per cent. The medical officer also says that there was only one case of V.D., that is among the staff the first week. There were no cases among the trainees. There were only four cases of drunkenness during the whole time.

I mention these things in order to emphasize the type of young men that we have in these training camps. They are the finest young men that we have in Canada; they represent the very flower of the manhood of this country.
The health of the men in camp might be compared with the health of men who did not get to camp. The great number of men who were turned down in my province and all over Canada for different defects was surprising to me. In the last war we know that tens of thousands of our young men were found not fit for service on account of certain ailments. One might think that from 1918 to 1940 there would have been some improvement in the health of our people, but I am satisfied, from the statistics obtained during this examination, that the state of health of the young men of Canada is just as deplorable now as it was then. Although the men were medically examined by their home doctors before they came to camp, after they arrived at camp, as the Prime Minister pointed ou-t the other day, fifteen per cent of them had to be rejected for medical unfitness. I would call it criminal negligence on the part of the authorities that we have not done more for the health of the greatest asset this country has, its young men. Mark you, these men were not all A-l; they were down to category C. If they had been examined for overseas service, the casualty list, so to speak, would have been much greater.
The minister this afternoon stated that the thirty-day period was not satisfactory. The period is not long enough; no man who knows anything about soldiering would say you can make a soldier in thirty days. One of the hardest things I had to do after training these men for thirty days and feeling that we could do something with them by further advanced training was to send them home feeling that perhaps we should never see them again in uniform and that the benefit of their training was lost. The men like the training, and I am pleased to hear the Minister of National Defence say that they have a plan on foot whereby men coming in for similar training will have the period extended.
As far as equipment is concerned, it was my personal opinion that probably the thirty-day limit had been set on account of lack of equipment, because there is no question that advanced training would have required more extensive equipment. In advanced training these men would need to know something about the Bren gun, and there are no Bren guns for training of this kind; there are no't enough for the active service force units. They would need anti-*tank guns and

The Address-Mr. Brooks
more gas masks and mechanical equipment .and rifles, and these are not available. We trust that these matters are being attended to by the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe); the question we would ask is, *"Why was not more done at an earlier date to- provide this equipment?"
Although the government has told our young men that they cannot be sent out of Canada for defence, that they can be used only for defence in this country, on their own initiative they are willing and anxious to serve outside Canada because they realize that that is where they should serve in order to defend this dominion. Answering a questionnaire, out of 660 men in my training centre those willing to serve in the Royal Canadian Navy numbered ninety-two, those willing to serve in the Royal Canadian Air Force numbered 266, those willing to serve in the active service force numbered 175, and those unwilling to serve anywhere numbered 127. Of the above, about 125 would like to get into the service right away; the others, as soon as they are required. This was prepared by my adjutant. He says:
Apparently none of this class was engaged in any industry purely for war. A number worked in plants where government contracts have been let.
That, of course, is characteristic of New Brunswick, as I stated at the beginning of my speech, because we have very few plants producing munitions in that province.
I was interested to hear the Minister of National Defence say this afternoon that our place is side by side with England wherever the fighting is. There is no fighting here in Canada, and therefore it should be impressed upon our young men that their duty lies [DOT]wherever the fighting may be. I have tried to impress this upon the young men with whom I come in contact because I think it is a patriotic duty which we ail should discharge.
I was pleased to hear the Prime Minister say that the policy of his government and the country is to push our war effort to the limit of our capacity. That is a big statement. We have a wonderful capacity in Canada; I do not suppose that there is any other country in the world with a greater. We had a wonderful capacity in the years from 1914 to 1918, and despite everything that may be said about our war effort at that time, I do not think any Canadian need feel ashamed of the part which Canada played from 1914 to 1918. But we are told that we were not a united people in the days from 1914 to 1918; we are told that we did not have the whole-hearted support of every section of the dominion. To-day, on the
contrary, we are told that we have this whole-hearted support of our war effort from one end of Canada to the other. Well, if our effort, which did not have the wholehearted support of every section of the country, as the government would like to make us believe, produced 500,000 volunteers in the period from 1914 to 1918, what must we say of the capacity of Canada to-day to produce an army 'under conditions such as we have been told now prevail? We are willing to wait and see if what has been told us is true. There are many who have grave doubts.
It is nearly six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and I do not wish to detain the house.

speechtext:
I thank the Prime Minister. May I say this in closing. We are justly proud to be side by side with Britain in the present defence of civilization and democracy; but listening to the speeches that have been delivered in this house during the last three or four days, I have not heard any mention of a gallant little nation which is also standing side by side with Britain and is to-day fighting for her very existence. I refer to Greece. Greece to-day is the British empire's only ally. She is fighting as fought the Greeks of old, thousands of years ago, at Salamis and Thermopylae. I remember reading as a boy these lines from Byron:
So fought the Greek of old,
So will he fight again:
Will not the self-same mold Bring forth the self-same men?
These self-same men we are proud to have as our ally to-day-men who are fighting to save as brave a country as any on earth.
We have been told that this will be a long war. It is hard for us to contemplate the prospect, all the harder when we read, as we do in to-night's newspapers, of such things as the fate that has befallen the historic city of Coventry in England, which has been practically ruined. Mr. Churchill, Britain's Prime Minister, assures us that we will fight on, unconquerable, until the curse of Hitler is lifted from the brows of men. It will no doubt take a long time; but when that curse is lifted, when the flag of freedom and of civilization floats once more proudly over the world, then the proudest boast we in Canada shall be able to make will be that we bore our full share in the defence of civilization, of home, of king and country.
Commonwealth Air Training

On motion of Mr. Adamson the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the house adjourned at six o'clock.
Monday, November 18, 1940.
